opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it was mostly a mismatch of timing and of what I was looking for at that stage, rather than anything being wrong with Adobe itself.

When I was there, I was still very early in figuring out what kind of research I wanted to do. Adobe Research had really strong people, and a lot of the work was naturally tied to products: imaging, editing, creative tools. That's a great environment if you know you want your research to land in something users touch. But I think I was more drawn to the fundamental questions. How do you learn good representations? What architectures actually scale? I wanted to chase things that might not have an obvious product use for years.

And I was young and a bit stubborn. I had my own ideas about what was interesting, and I didn't always fit them into the direction the team needed. Looking back, a lot of that was on me. I didn't know how to bridge my curiosity with what the group was trying to achieve. It wasn't that anyone held me back. It was more that I hadn't learned yet how to make a project work for both sides.

So I wouldn't call it a failure exactly. It taught me something about myself fairly early: I need an environment where open-ended exploration is the main job, not a side thing. That shaped a lot of my later choices, the places I went afterward, and eventually going back to academia. Sometimes the things that "don't work out" are the most useful signals you get.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the mismatch to timing, product-oriented work, and Saining’s preference for fundamental research. It does not cite Adobe’s artistic temperament as the reason.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I wouldn't frame it as things "not working out" — I think it was more that I figured out something about myself there.

When I was at Adobe, I was still fairly early in my research life, and the kind of work that mattered to the company was, understandably, very product-driven. You'd be looking at a problem and the first question was always, "how does this ship, and when?" That's a totally legitimate way to do research, and I learned a lot from the people there — they were incredibly good at taking ideas and making them actually work for real users.

But I realized that what I personally got excited about was a bit different. I liked the open-ended problems — the ones where you don't know whether the answer will be useful in six months, or three years, or ever. Things like architecture design, representation learning, questions about what the right fundamental building blocks are. That kind of work is hard to justify on a product roadmap, because you can't promise a result.

So it wasn't really a conflict, it was more of a mismatch in timescale and risk appetite. I wanted a place where I could sit with a problem for a long time, be wrong for a while, and not have to defend that every quarter. Going into a more academic-style environment gave me that freedom.

I'd also say — and I think this is important for younger researchers to hear — these experiences that "don't work out" are often the most useful ones. You don't learn what you want by only doing things that fit you perfectly. You learn it by trying something, feeling the friction, and asking why. Adobe was that for me. I came out of it with a much clearer sense of what kind of researcher I wanted to be, and I'm genuinely grateful for that.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the mismatch to Adobe’s product-driven priorities versus Xie’s preference for open-ended research; it does not mention the company’s artistic temperament.
